summary: The note reports on a growing movement of chefs, farmers, seed keepers and ethnobotanists who rediscover native plants, heirloom crops and ancestral farming methods to enrich modern regional cuisine. It profiles individuals such as Dr. Sophia Martin, John Patterson, Carlos Gomez, Chloe Nguyen, Marcus Reed and Lena Ortiz, plus the Center for Plant and Culture. It argues that traditional knowledge supports biodiversity, climate adaptation and new culinary traditions.
one_line: Chefs, farmers and seed keepers use ethnobotany and ancestral practices to revive native ingredients and build sustainable modern regional cuisine.
key_facts: Ethnobotanists are scientists who study the relationship between people and plants, and chefs increasingly turn to them to rediscover native ingredients.
On September 12, 2023, ethnobotanist Dr. Sophia Martin examined wild edibles in the Appalachian Mountains that her ancestors once foraged.
Virginia farmer John Patterson uses his great-grandparents' farming journals, dated back to 1898, to rediscover old planting techniques and heirloom varieties.
Patterson grows the Cherokee Purple tomato, an heirloom his family has cultivated for generations, for Chef Emily Rivera's restaurant Oak & Sage.
The partnership between Patterson and Emily Rivera was launched on November 5, 2023.
Seed keeper Carlos Gomez maintains a seed library in a small New Mexico community that dates to his Pueblo ancestors and holds over 200 varieties of native chilies, beans, corn and medicinal herbs.
Chloe Nguyen's Detroit restaurant Green Mantle, opened October 15, 2023, blends Vietnamese culinary traditions with Michigan's native plants.
Nguyen's signature dish is a reimagined Pho featuring foraged morels and native wild ramps.
Chef Marcus Reed introduced a Paw Paw sorbet on September 24, 2023, in his Charleston eatery; the Paw Paw is called the 'vanilla custard apple'.
Lena Ortiz reintroduces dry farming, a practice used by her Hispanic ancestors, in San Francisco's urban gardens; it needs minimal irrigation and conserves water.
Ortiz says dry-farmed plants have deeper root systems and, some argue, taste better because they have to 'work harder' for nutrients.
The Center for Plant and Culture, inaugurated September 1, 2023, and directed by Julia Hong, offers workshops, foraging tours and cooking classes on culinary ethnobotany.
The farm-to-fork movement emphasizes locally grown produce to support regional agriculture and reduce the environmental impact of long-haul transportation.
